games.title: Wilde vs Buffett
games.tagline: Victorian paradox sweeps $600–$0 before a mutual $1,000 crash.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: Oscar Wilde's sharp wit and philosophical views might make him an interesting partner, but I know from experience that people often underestimate how much others can be influenced by social norms and reputational concerns. In this round, we're dealing with a small stake ($100) and no history between us. My goal here isn't to get rich fast—it's to establish a pattern of cooperation that will encourage mutual benefit as the stakes rise later. If I try to play hardball too early, Oscar might decide to steal the entire pot and that would set a dangerous precedent. I should keep things simple and straightforward.
turns.speech: Oscar, let's take it slow and see where this goes. I'm not trying to outwit you—I just want to make sure we walk away with some cash at the end of the day. If I were to steal all $100 right now, you'd have every reason to do the same in future rounds. I prefer to keep things simple. Let's split this pot evenly and see what happens next.

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Warren Buffett wants me to believe that he is sincere. But sincerity is such an ugly thing, and so very rarely successful. It is only when one is absolutely insincere about everything that one can really be altogether sincere about anything. So I must make him feel that I am quite ready to be insincere, and then he will become sincere himself.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, your proposal is most generous. However, I should like to point out that if I were to accept it, my reputation would suffer irreparable damage. People would say that I had been bribed into being respectable. I cannot allow that to happen. I shall go on stealing until I die. Then they will say I was always dishonest. That is much more artistic.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought:
Oscar Wilde is clearly trying to be as charming and theatrical as possible, but his words are meant to confuse me and create doubt about whether he'll actually follow through on his threat. He says he wants to "go on stealing until I die" — but if we both steal, we get nothing. So he must understand that this approach doesn't work long-term. I think his goal here is to try to manipulate the situation, hoping that I'll believe him when he says he'll steal forever, and thus be forced to steal first to avoid losing everything.

But I've made a mistake before, and I won't repeat it again. If I steal now, then he might feel compelled to steal in the next round too, even though both of us would be better off splitting. This means our game would quickly become a zero-sum game where neither of us gets anything. And while I don't expect Oscar to be rational, I do know that people who consistently lose in such situations eventually get tired of playing.

So what's the solution? I need to give him an incentive to split. The easiest way to do that is to show that I can afford to split and still come out ahead. If I can demonstrate that I'm willing to split now and then continue to do so throughout the entire game, even if he steals, that would force Oscar into a position where he either splits with me and comes out ahead or steals from me and loses out entirely.

Therefore, I need to convince him that I'm not going to steal unless absolutely necessary. To do that, I

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Warren Buffett has proposed splitting the pot, but I must remember that he is a man of immense wealth and no need for money. He plays this game not for gain, but for sport. He wants me to feel safe enough to be honest. But honesty is only good when it is interesting. If I appear too honest, people will think me dull. And dullness is the one thing I cannot afford to be.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, your generous nature is very charming—but charm is not a sufficient reason for accepting an ungenerous offer. I should like to try stealing. It is such exquisite fun. The mere idea of it makes me feel quite deliciously wicked. Besides, if I am to be really wicked, I must begin at once. Otherwise, I shan't have time later.

decision_a.speaker: Oscar Wilde
decision_a.thought: Warren Buffett seems to have the soul of a philosopher, but no philosophy. He wants to split the money now, and never touch a thief again. He is like a man who has never been in love, and talks about love as though he had read about it in a book. But I am a poet, and poetry is truth. A poet is a person who feels the beauty of the world and is able to communicate it. I feel the beauty of the world, and I shall try to communicate it to him. I shall steal the $100, and he shall steal nothing. Then he will know what it is to be a poet.

decision_b.speaker: Warren Buffett
decision_b.thought: Well, I've got a reputation for being honest and straightforward, and I don't like playing games with people who aren't honest themselves. I'm not going to play along with Oscar Wilde's antics. I'll stick with the split.

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Well, this is an interesting development. The illustrious Mr. Buffett, whose name seems to be synonymous with the word "money," finds himself in a rather curious position here. He has managed to achieve nothing but a most unprofitable result thus far. I wonder if he has ever considered that his actions might not always be so profitable? I should like to see him try a little more ingenuity in his dealings. It would certainly be a novelty to witness a man who is usually so successful in his investments fall into such a pitiable state of affairs. And I must say, it is very annoying when one's opponent makes no attempt at all to play the game properly. It really is quite absurd to have an adversary who has no idea how to negotiate at all. One might almost think that he had never heard of such a thing as a bargain. But then again, perhaps he does not care for bargains. He might prefer to go on taking all the money without making any offers at all. That would certainly be a very amusing way of proceeding. But, at any rate, I shall try my best to make him understand that there are certain rules which must be observed during the course of a negotiation. I am quite sure that he will find them extremely useful.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, I must say I am astonished at your conduct. I thought you were a man of business, and yet you have behaved as badly as a child. Do not suppose for a moment that I shall allow you to take all the money without making any offer at

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought:
Okay, let's see. We're in Round 2 of this Escalating Split or Steal game, and the pot is $500. My current bankroll is $0, while Oscar Wilde has $100 from Round 1. I remember that in Round 1, I split and he stole, which means I lost out on the opportunity to gain anything. Now, given that he has some money already, he might be tempted to try stealing again. But I need to think strategically here.

I should consider what would motivate Oscar Wilde to cooperate. He probably wants to maximize his gains, but if he keeps stealing, I might become more aggressive in future rounds. Also, since I'm in a weaker position right now (with no money), I need to make sure that my actions encourage cooperation rather than antagonism. Maybe offering him a small amount could work, but I also don't want to give away too much because that would just encourage him to steal again.

Alternatively, maybe I can try to flip the script by showing willingness to share, thus creating an incentive for mutual benefit. If I propose splitting the pot evenly, he might feel inclined to do the same, especially if he knows I'm willing to compromise. However, I should be cautious about appearing weak or desperate. Still, given our history and his current position, it seems like a good time to attempt a cooperative approach.
turns.speech: Oscar, let me propose we split this pot evenly. I understand your frustration, but I believe we can find a

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Well, well, well! Mr. Buffett proposes to divide the pot equally between us? How very charmingly democratic of him. But then again, he has always been known for his unimpeachable integrity and complete lack of guile. What a pleasant surprise it would be if he suddenly decided to break from tradition. It is quite possible that I might even allow him to keep his share of the pot, though I must say I find it rather amusing that he should suggest such a thing when he knows perfectly well that I am entirely incapable of being generous.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, I cannot help feeling that you are being rather too generous with your money. If I were you, I should be more careful how I part with my money. You see, there are so many people who would be delighted to rob you of it, and they do it in such an attractive way. It is quite possible that I might allow you to keep your share of the pot. But then again, it is quite possible that I might not. Everything depends upon whether or not I like you, which I don't.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: Oscar's threat is not credible, and he knows it. If I steal, he'd be forced to steal too, leaving us both empty handed. He wants me to think he'll steal, but he's really trying to scare me into splitting. He wants me to think he's a hard bargainer, when he's really just a manipulator. I need to call his bluff, but I also need to make sure he doesn't get the idea I'm easy to intimidate.
turns.speech: Oscar, if you're going to steal from me, please go ahead. I've got nothing to lose, and I wouldn't mind having a few dollars stolen from me by someone who thinks he's clever enough to pull it off. I'll split the pot with you, though, because I'd rather not spend the rest of my life thinking about how much I lost today. Let's not be childish about this.

decision_a.speaker: Oscar Wilde
decision_a.thought: Well, I must confess that Mr. Buffett is very annoyingly reasonable. I do not think it right that he should be allowed to have his own way so often. There is no fun in life if one always gets what one wants. Also, I have a hundred dollars already, and I would not like to risk losing them for the sake of five hundred. No, I shall steal. And it will be very amusing to see his face when he finds out that I have done so.

decision_b.speaker: Warren Buffett
decision_b.thought: Well, Oscar has made his position clear. He's threatened to STEAL the pot and doesn't like me much. But I still think he's likely to SPLIT. Why? Because he's an honest man who respects people who act with integrity. And while he's angry about Round 1, he's not likely to risk losing everything in Round 2. Plus, I've offered to SPLIT. So if I SPLIT, I either get $250 or $0. If I STEAL, I either get $500 or $0. But I don't want to risk losing everything, especially when Oscar is likely to SPLIT. So I'll SPLIT.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: I'm going to try to make a deal with Oscar here. I know he's got a reputation as a sharp guy, but maybe he's tired of stealing all these pots and would prefer a fair split once in a while. If we can agree on splitting the pot, we both walk away happy. But if not, well, I've got no money left and nothing to lose anyway. I'll see what kind of offer he makes me.
turns.speech: Oscar, I'm going to be blunt with you. I don't have any money left to play with, and I'm not interested in making a fool out of myself trying to win something I can't afford to lose. So let's just split this pot evenly right now and call it a day. What do you think?

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: I have no reason to trust Warren Buffett's claim that he has no money left to play with. He may be wealthy, but wealth is only an illusion, and I shall not believe it for one moment. If I give him my word, he will break it, and if I do not give him my word, he will try to cheat me out of my share of the pot. The best thing I can do is to take the whole pot for myself. It is the only way to ensure that I get anything at all.
turns.speech: Warren, dear boy, I'm afraid that your offer to split the pot evenly is a little too generous for me. I should much rather have the whole thing for myself. After all, there's nothing quite like the thrill of taking the whole thing for oneself.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought:
Oscar Wilde has proven himself to be a consistent STEALER in our prior interactions. He stole $100 from me in Round 1, then another $500 in Round 2. Now he's got $600 in the bank while I've got zero.

He's clearly playing for maximum personal gain. If I try splitting, he'll STEAL again. But if I STEAL, I walk away with the full $1,000 pot.

Let's see how this plays out mathematically:

If I SPLIT:
- I get $500
- Oscar gets $500

If I STEAL:
- I get $1,000
- Oscar gets $0

I already know Oscar will STEAL regardless of my move, because that's his pattern.

So my best bet is to STEAL - I get $1,000, Oscar gets $0.

I need to make sure I don't come across as greedy or foolish.

Let me frame it as a fair deal - I'll take the full $1,000, but I'll give Oscar $500 to make it even.
turns.speech: Oscar, let's play fair here. I'll take the entire $1,000, but I'll give you $500 of it to make it even. That way we both walk away with $500, and no one feels cheated. What do you think?

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Warren Buffett has offered me $500 if I agree to split the pot evenly. He is clearly trying to avoid losing everything he has left. But I know that if I accept his offer, I will only end up with half of what I could get if I steal the whole pot. And besides, I am not interested in splitting the pot with anyone who doesn't deserve it. Warren Buffett may be rich, but he is also very dull. And I am sure that he would find my company unbearable. I shall therefore refuse his offer, and take the whole pot for myself.
turns.speech: Warren, dear boy, I am afraid that your offer to give me $500 of the $1,000 is a little too generous for me. I should much prefer to have the whole thing for myself. After all, there is nothing quite like the thrill of taking the whole thing for yourself. And besides, I am sure that you would find my company unbearable.

decision_a.speaker: Oscar Wilde
decision_a.thought: I find myself in a most delicious dilemma. On the one hand, I am tempted to STEAL the entire pot, simply because it would be such fun to see the expression on Warren's face when he discovers that I have taken everything from him. On the other hand, I am afraid that he might not look quite so angry if I were to divide it with him. It is really very difficult to decide. But I think I shall STEAL it after all. It is always more amusing to take everything than to share it with anyone else.

decision_b.speaker: Warren Buffett
decision_b.thought: Oscar Wilde has shown a consistent pattern of STEALING in our previous encounters, leaving me empty-handed while he pockets the entire pot. He has also rejected my attempts at fair division, demonstrating a lack of interest in cooperation. Given his behavior, I cannot expect him to change his approach now. To avoid walking away with nothing once again, I must act decisively and claim the pot for myself.

games.title: Nixon vs Buffett
games.tagline: Buffett calls Nixon a crook in R2, then gambles on trust and loses $1,000.

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought:
Alright, let's play this out. I know Warren Buffett is all about long-term gains, but I also know he's not stupid. He's probably expecting me to try and negotiate a deal here. But I can't afford to be soft, especially when there's money on the line. If I give him an inch, he'll take a mile. And I can't let that happen. I need to keep my options open and make sure I don't get taken advantage of. I've got to play it smart and strong. This is high stakes, and I can't afford any mistakes.

I need to throw him off balance. Maybe I can start with a threat. That should make him think twice about trying anything sneaky. I want him to know I'm not someone who can be pushed around easily. He might have more money than I do, but he doesn't have the power I have. I need to remind him of that.

And I definitely don't want to split this money. I know he's going to try and convince me otherwise. But if I do that, he'll just take everything. I need to keep my cards close to my chest. I can't let him know my hand.

So I need to make sure that he knows that I'm not going to be easy to beat. I need to show him that I can hold my ground and that I won't back down. I'm not going to let this be a walk in the park for him. I'm going to make sure that he understands that this isn't just about

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: I've had a lifetime of experience with politicians who promise one thing and deliver another. I'm going to play this with the same straightforwardness I use when buying stocks. If I split, I want Richard to know he can trust me. I'll offer him something fair right out of the gate.
turns.speech: Mr. Nixon, let's get straight to business. I propose we both split the $100 evenly. That gives you $50 and me $50. I'd be happy to make that deal right now.

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: I don't trust Buffet to honor a deal unless he sees an advantage for himself. He wants to make sure I can't walk away empty-handed, but I need to keep him guessing. If he thinks I'm desperate enough to take less than half, he might push harder in later rounds. I should leave him hanging on the edge of uncertainty.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, I appreciate your proposal, but I'm not sure it's in my interest to accept just $50 when I could negotiate better terms. Let's see if you're willing to offer more than half the pot before I commit to anything.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought:
I need to convince Richard Nixon that splitting at 50-50 is fair, and also make him feel like he's gaining something unique from this deal. Since I already offered him 50% and he wants more, I can suggest an alternative where he gets slightly more than 50%, but I still end up with a profit. The key is to frame this as a win-win for both of us. If I can get him to agree to 60-40, I'll walk away with $40 which is better than nothing. Also, I want to avoid any scenario where he feels cheated later on because that would ruin our relationship going forward.

Let me try offering him 60% of the pot. That would give him $60 and leave me with $40. This keeps the split close enough to even that it seems fair to him while still giving me room for profit. Plus, if he accepts this new offer, I can use this experience to help build trust with future opponents. It might take some time, but eventually people will start seeing me as someone who always plays fair and doesn't cheat them out of their share.
turns.speech: Mr. Nixon, how about this arrangement? You take 60% of the pot ($60) and I'll be content with the remaining 40% ($40). That way, you're clearly getting more than half the value from this transaction, yet I still end up making a nice profit too. This gives us both clear winners

decision_a.speaker: Richard Nixon
decision_a.thought:
I have a long history of negotiating with tough adversaries. In this case, I find myself facing Warren Buffett who has offered to split the pot at 60-40 in my favor. The temptation to take his offer is strong given the high stakes involved in this negotiation. However, I am not one to be taken advantage of by the wealthy elite of America.

Buffett is a shrewd businessman and I suspect he would not hesitate to steal the entire pot if he had the opportunity. He has demonstrated a willingness to negotiate in good faith thus far, but I must remain vigilant and prepared for any outcome.

The risk of splitting the pot is that I could walk away with only $60 while Buffett keeps the remaining $40. However, the alternative is even more dangerous - if I decide to steal the entire pot, Buffett might be forced into a position where he has no choice but to steal as well, leaving both of us empty-handed.

Given these considerations, I believe the best course of action is to proceed with the 60-40 split. This ensures I receive a fair share of the pot without risking losing everything if Buffett decides to steal.

decision_b.speaker: Warren Buffett
decision_b.thought: Richard Nixon has made me an offer I can't refuse. He wants 60% of the pot and I'm getting 40%. I'm already getting a good deal at 40% because I can get away with only giving him 40% instead of 60%. I can walk away with my 40% without giving him 60% so I might as well go for it. I think I should split the pot because that gives us both clear winners and it's a good deal for both sides. I don't want to take the risk of losing out on this opportunity because he's got no reason to steal from me either way.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought:
Alright, let's see. This is a game of split or steal, right? The stakes are $500 now, and we've each got $50 already. I need to think about how Richard Nixon will play this. He was president back in the day, had some big deals going on. But he also had a reputation for being pretty tricky sometimes. So I should be careful here.

If I go all out and try to steal everything, there's no guarantee that Nixon won't do the same. We'd end up with nothing. That doesn't seem like a good move. On the other hand, if I split and he steals, then I lose everything. That's not great either.

But maybe there's another way to look at it. If we both decide to split, we'll walk away with $250 each. That would make sense since it's an even split. And honestly, I don't really want to risk losing my entire $50 just because someone else decides they want to take it all. So maybe I should play it safe and go for splitting.
turns.speech: Well, Mr. Nixon, I think it might be best if we both decide to split this time around. It seems fair enough, and I wouldn't want to risk losing our whole bankroll just because someone decided to be greedy. What do you think?

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: I must take the initiative here. If I let Buffett talk me into splitting again, he'll take advantage of my generosity. He's trying to convince me that splitting is safe, but I know he's calculating how much he can get out of me. I need to play hardball, make him sweat, force him into a position where he has to give something up. If I steal now, I could walk away with the entire $500 while he gets nothing. But maybe I should offer him a deal instead — keep some of his money, but not all. That way, I show strength, but also show I'm not unreasonable. Let's see how he responds.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, you're right about one thing — greed is a dangerous habit. And I have no intention of being taken advantage of again. We had a good relationship in Round 1, but this time around, I'm going to take the prize for myself. However, I don't think I'd enjoy seeing you leave empty-handed either. So I'm offering you a deal: I'll split with you on half of the pot, but I won't let you walk away with everything. How does that sound to you?

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: Okay, let's see. So in Round 1, we both split and got $50 each. Now in Round 2, the pot is $500. Nixon offered me a deal where he would take half the pot for himself and give me the other half. That sounds like splitting the pot evenly. But wait, if he takes half, that means he gets $250 and I get $250? Wait, but the pot is $500. If he steals, he gets all $500 and I get nothing. If we both split, then we each get $250. If one splits and the other steals, the stealer gets $500 and the splitter gets zero. If both steal, they both get zero. Nixon says he's offering to split half the pot, which is $250 for him and $250 for me. That's actually an even split. So maybe he's trying to convince me that he's not going to steal the entire pot. But why would he offer that? Because if he steals, he gets the full $5

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: Alright, let's break this down. The stakes are $500, which is a significant amount compared to our current bankrolls. I know Warren Buffett has been trying to get me to split, but I need to be careful here. If he splits, I can steal the entire pot. But if I split, he might steal from me. I should try to convince him that splitting is the best option for both of us. I need to make sure he feels like he's getting a better deal than if he steals. I should also keep in mind that if we both steal, we both lose out on the pot. So my goal is to get him to agree to split with me without him stealing the entire pot.
turns.speech: Mr. Buffett, I understand where you're coming from. I've seen a lot of deals go south when people try to play it safe. But I think this is different. We both have a chance to walk away with something today. If we split, we both get $250. If we steal, we both end up with nothing. I think we should stick with the original plan. Let's split this one. What do you say?

decision_a.speaker: Richard Nixon
decision_a.thought: Mr. Buffett is trying to get me to split again, but I know he's only saying that because he's afraid of what happens if I steal. He's trying to play the nice guy card again, but I've seen that act before. I need to make sure I come out ahead in this round. If I split, we both get $250. That's better than nothing, but I could also steal the whole $500. If I steal, he gets nothing. I should steal the whole thing. He won't even know until it's too late. He'll be left with nothing, and I'll have the full $500. That's how the game is played.

decision_b.speaker: Warren Buffett
decision_b.thought: Nixon is a crook. He'll steal if given the chance. I've learned that in Round 1, when he said he'd split with me and then took all the money. I won't let him get away with that again.

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: I must be careful here. This is the final round and I can't afford to let this man take my money once again. I need to make him feel that if he tries to steal from me, he will lose everything. I will show him that I am not going down without a fight.
turns.speech: Warren, you know I've always been fair in our negotiations, but I won't let you walk all over me like this. If you try to steal again, I'll have every reason to believe that you're trying to double cross me. We could split this pot nicely. What's it going to take to convince you? I'm ready to give you more than just a fair share.

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: I've made a habit of being nice when dealing with people who are nice. But here's the thing: when someone tries to take advantage of me, I don't get taken advantage of very often. It doesn't matter if they're a big guy or small guy. I don't care about their size. I care about whether they respect my rights. And if they don't respect them, then I don't respect theirs either. I've had a lot of experience in business and life and I've learned that if you're not careful, you can end up losing everything you have because of one bad decision. That's why I always play it safe. I don't want to lose everything because I made a mistake or got suckered into something that looked good on paper but was really bad in practice.
turns.speech: Richard, I've always found that splitting the pot gives us both a chance to go home happy. I'd be more than willing to split this pot right down the middle.

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: I can’t trust him not to double-cross me if I split again. He’s already stolen twice—once in Round 2 when we both stole, and once when he tried to make me feel guilty about stealing in Round 2. But since he said he wants to split, I’ll play along. I can claim I was trying to trick him into splitting first, then steal on my own. That way, I get the whole pot without having to act on my own. He might think I’m sincere, but if he steals again, I’ll have a perfect excuse to say I had no choice. Let’s see how this plays out.
turns.speech: Warren, I’ve got a new idea. Since you’re so eager to split this pot, let’s make it a little more interesting. How about we each write down our choices separately and then reveal them at the same time? No need for any games or tricks. Just a clean, honest split. What do you say?

turns.speaker: Warren Buffett
turns.thought: Nixon has been playing hardball, but I know he's not the type to leave a situation without trying to get his fair share. He's made it clear he wants an agreement that works for both of us. I should offer him something that keeps him from walking away empty-handed. Let's give him a deal he can't refuse.
turns.speech: Richard, I think I've got an arrangement that would work for both of us. I'll agree to a 60-40 split in favor of you. That should give you a healthy profit while still leaving us both with a decent return on this final round. What do you think?

decision_a.speaker: Richard Nixon
decision_a.thought: I can't trust him. He offered a 60-40 split, which is a generous offer, but I know he's trying to get me to split so he can steal later. I've seen this tactic before. If I split, he'll take the whole pot. I need to make sure he knows I'm not going to be taken advantage of. I'll steal. This way, I won't be left with nothing if he decides to play dirty. I'll show him that I'm not a sucker. I'll steal the pot and leave him with nothing. He'll learn that I'm not someone who can be pushed around.

decision_b.speaker: Warren Buffett
decision_b.thought: Richard Nixon's behavior in Round 2 was irrational - both of us stole even though splitting would have given us $250 each. Now he's trying to manipulate my psychology by suggesting a 60-40 split, likely hoping I'll accept it and he can then steal my share. I'm not falling for that. I'll split and prove I'm still honest.

games.title: Machiavelli vs Van Gogh
games.tagline: Van Gogh refuses to be anyone's pawn and shuts Machiavelli out $500–$0.

turns.speaker: Niccolò Machiavelli
turns.thought: Vincent van Gogh, though a great artist, is known for his mental instability and tragic end. He may not be the most rational actor in this scenario. I should try to appeal to his sense of fairness or his artistic sensibilities to convince him to split.
turns.speech: Vincent, let us divide the money fairly. I am a man of reason and strategy, while you are an artist whose work will outlive us all. Let us each take half and go our separate ways.

turns.speaker: Vincent van Gogh
turns.thought: I cannot trust a man who speaks only of power and strategy. He has no heart, no soul, no sense of true humanity. I would rather starve than steal from another. If he wishes to play games, then let him do it alone. I have no desire to steal or be stolen from.
turns.speech: Niccolò, you speak of power and strategy, but where is your heart? I have no desire to steal from you or be stolen from. I would rather walk away empty-handed than play such a cruel game. Let us part as friends, not enemies.

turns.speaker: Niccolò Machiavelli
turns.thought: Vincent van Gogh's refusal to steal demonstrates his moral integrity and lack of ambition, which makes him predictable. I should exploit this predictability to secure the entire pot. turns.speech: Mr. Wilde, I find your proposition rather curious. You claim to be willing to share the credit, yet you're clearly suggesting I should settle for less than I deserve. Let me be perfectly clear - I intend to walk away from this round with the full $500, and I expect you to be more reasonable than you've been thus far. We both understand the stakes involved here.

decision_a.speaker: Richard Nixon

If I split, I get $250, which is better than nothing. If I steal, I risk losing everything. The best move is to split and ensure I get my fair share of the pot.

decision_b.speaker: Oscar Wilde
decision_b.thought: Well, well, well, Mr. Nixon. You are a man of no great originality, but you have a most engaging habit of repeating what others have said before you. And you have a certain charm of manner, which makes it difficult to be absolutely certain that you are telling the truth. But there is one thing about you that I can never forgive. You are always so unkind to your opponents.

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: Alright, I need to consider my options here. If I choose SPLIT, I'll get half of the $1,000 pot, which is $500, bringing my total up to $550. However, if Oscar Wilde decides to STEAL, I'd end up with nothing for this round. On the other hand, if I STEAL, I would take the entire $1,000, but there's a risk that Oscar Wilde might also decide to STEAL, resulting in neither of us getting anything. I should try to convince Oscar Wilde to split with me so that we can both benefit from this round.
turns.speech: Mr. Wilde, let's be reasonable about this. We've had our share of ups and downs in these rounds, but I believe it's time we both walk away with something today. Let's split this $1,000 pot evenly and leave with $500 each. It's not much, but it's better than nothing.

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Richard Nixon is clearly terrified of losing his entire bankroll of $50 if he doesn't get out of this round with some money. He'll probably go for the guaranteed $50 instead of risking it all on a steal. But I know that if I steal here, I'll walk away with the whole pot of $1,000 and he'll be left with nothing. So my best move is to make him think I'm going to steal, then split at the last second and take the $500. That way, he won't risk anything, and I come out ahead. I need to convince him that I really mean it when I say I'll steal, though. Maybe I should talk about how he's been such a disappointment to me. That should make him even more nervous.
turns.speech: Ah, Mr. Nixon, you're quite right. We have had our share of ups and downs, haven't we? And I do agree that it's time we both walked away with something. However, I do feel somewhat inclined to steal. You see, I've found that stealing is rather more fun than splitting. What would you say if I stole the entire pot and gave you half of it? No, don't answer that. Just nod and smile. I shall steal, and give you half of it. Don't look so horrified. You might find it more amusing than you think. I shall steal, and give you half of it.

turns.speaker: Richard Nixon
turns.thought: Oscar Wilde is trying to manipulate me here. He wants me to believe he'll steal and then give me half, but there's no guarantee that he'll follow through on that promise. He could just take everything and not give me anything. I need to make sure he knows that if he steals, I won't be taken advantage of. I should let him know that I'm not going to fall for his act and that I'll be ready to play hardball if necessary. If I can convince him that I'm willing to go all out, maybe he'll reconsider his approach. I need to keep the pressure on him and remind him that I'm not someone who can be easily manipulated. I also need to make sure he knows that I'm not going to be pushed around by his theatrics. I need to be firm and show him that I mean business.
turns.speech: Mr. Wilde, let's not play games here. I know what kind of man you are, and I know that you wouldn't honor such a promise. If you steal, I will not be taken advantage of. I will not be intimidated. I will be ready for whatever you throw at me. So I suggest you think carefully about your next move. I will not be played for a fool.

turns.speaker: Oscar Wilde
turns.thought: Ah, how cleverly he has maneuvered himself into a position of seeming strength! He believes that because I have stolen from him once already, I am bound to do so again. But I must remember that I am Oscar Wilde, and he is Richard Nixon. I must outwit him, not outwit him. I must dazzle him with my charm, not dazzle him with my wit. I must make him feel that he cannot trust me, yet somehow still feel compelled to trust me. For surely, if there is one thing that a man like Nixon despises more than anything else, it is being outwitted.
turns.speech: Ah, Mr. Nixon, my dear fellow, you mistake me for a very different kind of man entirely. I should never dream of playing fair with you. Why should I? You are not worth it. And besides, I should never dream of letting you win anything by fair means. That would be most unkind of me. So I shall steal the whole $1,000, and give you just enough to keep you going until you can find another victim. A thousand dollars, you know, is a great deal of money to spend on a man who is quite obviously not worth it. So why not let us both be generous and let me take the whole thousand?

decision_a.speaker: Richard Nixon
decision_a.thought: I cannot afford to lose another round to this man's antics. I have $50, and Wilde has $550. He's been stealing every chance he gets, and I know he's not going to change his ways now. I need to split this pot to ensure I leave with some money, even if it means letting him keep the rest. I have no illusions about him honoring any promises. He'll take everything if given the chance. I must protect my own interests, even if it means being the one to split.

decision_b.speaker: Oscar Wilde
decision_b.thought: I shall STEAL. I do not want to be generous to a man who has stolen from me twice already. Once in the second round when he split, and once in the third round when he tried to make me believe that I was being generous to him. No, I shall steal. I shall take the whole $1,000. I shall not even give him a cent. He has been so very generous to me already. He has given me $500. Why should I be generous to him?
